metadata.description: Advanced logical reasoning training data including predicate logic, modal logic, temporal logic, and formal reasoning systems

reasoning_steps: Step 1: Universal instantiation on premise 1 with x = Socrates
Step 2: Human(Socrates) → Mortal(Socrates)
Step 3: Apply modus ponens with premise 2: Human(Socrates)
Step 4: Conclude: Mortal(Socrates)

premises: □(P → Q) - It is necessary that if P then Q
reasoning_steps: Step 1: From □(P → Q), in all possible worlds: P → Q
Step 2: From □P, in all possible worlds: P is true
Step 3: By universal modus ponens across all worlds: Q is true in all worlds
Step 4: Therefore: □Q (Q is necessary)

premises: F(P) - Eventually P will be true
G(¬P) - P will always be false
reasoning_steps: Step 1: F(P) means there exists future time t where P(t) is true
Step 2: G(¬P) means for all future times t, ¬P(t) is true
Step 3: This creates contradiction: P(t) ∧ ¬P(t) for some time t
Step 4: By principle of non-contradiction: ⊥ (contradiction)

premises: ∃x∀y(Loves(x,y)) - There exists someone who loves everyone
reasoning_steps: Step 1: Let a be the witness for ∃x, so ∀y(Loves(a,y))
Step 2: For any arbitrary person b, we have Loves(a,b)
Step 3: Since a exists and Loves(a,b), we have ∃x(Loves(x,b))
Step 4: Since b was arbitrary, ∀y∃x(Loves(x,y))
Step 1: Case analysis on the disjunction
Step 2: Case 1: P ∧ Q is true. Then P is true and Q is true
Step 3: From P true: (P ∨ R), (P ∨ S) are true
Step 4: From Q true: (Q ∨ R), (Q ∨ S) are true
Step 5: Case 2: R ∧ S is true. Then R is true and S is true
Step 6: From R, S true: all four disjunctions are satisfied
Step 7: In both cases, conclusion holds

premises: ◊□P - It is possible that P is necessary
reasoning_steps: Step 1: ◊□P means there exists world w where □P holds in w
Step 2: □◊P means in all worlds, P is possibly true
Step 3: Counter-model: Consider worlds w1, w2 where only w1 satisfies P
Step 4: At w1: □P is false (P not necessary), so ◊□P is false
Step 5: But ◊P is true at both worlds, so □◊P could be true
Step 6: This shows the inference is invalid in general
advanced_logical_examples.conclusion: Invalid inference - requires specific modal conditions

premises: ∀x(Px → Qx) - For all x, if P(x) then Q(x)
∃x(Px ∧ Rx) - There exists x such that P(x) and R(x)
reasoning_steps: Step 1: Let a be witness for ∃x(Px ∧ Rx), so Pa ∧ Ra
Step 2: From premise 1 by universal instantiation: Pa → Qa
Step 3: From Pa ∧ Ra, we extract Pa
Step 4: By modus ponens on Pa → Qa and Pa: Qa
Step 5: We have Ra from step 1, so Qa ∧ Ra
Step 6: Therefore ∃x(Qx ∧ Rx) with witness a
advanced_logical_examples.logical_form: Existential Instantiation + Universal Instantiation + Modus Ponens

advanced_logical_examples.problem: X(P U Q) ⊢ XF(Q) (Next Until implies Next Eventually)
premises: X(P U Q) - In the next state, P holds until Q
reasoning_steps: Step 1: X(P U Q) means at time t+1: (P U Q)
Step 2: (P U Q) at t+1 means Q will eventually be true from t+1 onwards
Step 3: This means F(Q) is true at time t+1
Step 4: Therefore X(F(Q)) is true at current time t
Step 5: Since XF(Q) is equivalent to X(F(Q)): XF(Q)

premises: ¬∀x(Px) - It is not the case that all x have property P
reasoning_steps: Step 1: ¬∀x(Px) means it's false that every x satisfies Px
Step 2: This means there exists at least one x that doesn't satisfy Px
Step 3: Formally: there exists x such that ¬Px
Step 4: Therefore: ∃x(¬Px)

premises: K_a(P ∧ Q) - Agent a knows that both P and Q are true
reasoning_steps: Step 1: K_a(P ∧ Q) means in all worlds agent a considers possible, P ∧ Q holds
Step 2: If P ∧ Q holds in all these worlds, then P holds in all these worlds
Step 3: Similarly, Q holds in all these worlds
Step 4: Therefore K_a(P) and K_a(Q) both hold
Step 5: Conclusion: K_a(P) ∧ K_a(Q)
